summary: Aversive medication for alcohol use disorder that causes a severe reaction if alcohol is consumed. Not useful for cravings; requires abstinence, motivation, and informed consent.
description: Disulfiram is an aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor used for long-term treatment of moderate to severe alcohol use disorder. It blocks metabolism of alcohol at the acetaldehyde stage, leading to flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, and hypotension if alcohol is consumed. Severe reactions can include arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse. It does not reduce cravings directly; instead it works through negative reinforcement and requires good adherence and motivation. Disulfiram must never be given to someone who is intoxicated or without their full knowledge. It should be combined with psychosocial treatments and careful medical monitoring.
patient_summary: Disulfiram helps people stay away from drinking by making alcohol cause an intense sick reaction. If you drink while on this medicine, you can get flushing, nausea, vomiting, feeling faint, or chest discomfort. The effect can last up to 1–2 weeks after the last dose, so even a small amount of alcohol can trigger problems. It doesn’t reduce cravings and works best when you’re motivated and supported in treatment.

primary.context: Aversive therapy; requires abstinence, insight, and motivation. Does not reduce cravings.

contraindications.contraindication: Severe myocardial disease or coronary occlusion
Hypersensitivity to disulfiram or thiuram derivatives

precautions: Severe reactions if any alcohol is consumed (even small amounts).
Reaction may include flushing, pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, difficulty breathing, hypotension.
Severe cases: arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse, seizures, death.
Avoid hidden alcohol in cough syrups, sauces, vinegar, mouthwash, aftershave.

interactions.action: Strict avoidance of all alcohol and alcohol-containing products

special_populations.pregnancy: Limited data; generally avoid unless needed for acute withdrawal.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: No formal taper required, but adverse reactions to alcohol may persist for 1–2 weeks after stopping.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Long-term treatment of moderate to severe alcohol use disorder in motivated adults who can remain abstinent.
items: {link:condition:alcohol-use-disorder:Alcohol Use Disorder}: Aversive therapy to support abstinence.

sections.heading: What People Often Notice

quotes: Just knowing I’ll get sick keeps me from drinking.
I had one slip and felt awful for hours.
It works best when I check in with my counselor.
I needed reminders about hidden alcohol in products.

sections.intro: Used in motivated adults who want to avoid relapse.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
key_points: Begins working ~12 hours after first dose.
Reactions can occur for 1–2 weeks after stopping.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Never administer to a patient who is intoxicated or without their full knowledge.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Metallic/garlic taste, fatigue, drowsiness; serious risks include hepatitis, neuropathy, and severe disulfiram–alcohol reaction.

items.action: Strict avoidance of all alcohol and alcohol-containing products

sections.heading: Stopping Safely
sections.text: No formal taper required, but adverse reactions to alcohol may persist for 1–2 weeks after stopping.

sections.heading: Dosing Information

adult.alcohol_use_disorder: 250–500 mg once daily for 1–2 weeks, then 250 mg daily as typical maintenance (max 500 mg/day).

sections.simple_explanation: Usually one pill per day after several days without drinking.

sections.heading: Special Groups
sections.text: Use with caution in liver disease, cardiac disease, seizure disorders, diabetes, and hypothyroidism.
sections.pregnancy: Limited data; generally avoid unless needed for acute withdrawal.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase leading to acetaldehyde accumulation when alcohol is consumed, causing aversive symptoms.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment
sections.text: An aversive, motivation-dependent option for alcohol use disorder when craving-reducing agents (naltrexone, acamprosate) are inadequate or not tolerated.

faqs.q: What happens if I drink while taking disulfiram?
faqs.a: You may get a severe reaction with flushing, pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, and low blood pressure. It can be dangerous.

faqs.q: How long after stopping is it still risky?
faqs.a: Reactions can occur for up to 1–2 weeks after the last dose.
No. It works by making drinking very unpleasant, not by reducing urges.

faqs.q: Can I use mouthwash or sauces that contain alcohol?
faqs.a: Avoid all products with alcohol, even small amounts, including mouthwash and cooking sauces.
